# Herbs on a Small Balcony

A balcony garden starts small. These notes cover the pots, the light and the watering, in that order.

### Part one: pots

Terracotta pots breathe through their walls, so the soil dries evenly and the roots stay healthy. They also crack in a hard frost, which means they come inside in winter. Plastic pots hold water longer and sit lighter on a railing. Either works, provided the pot drains.

I drilled extra holes in my first plastic pot with a hand drill. It took ten minutes and saved the basil.

### Part two: light

Most kitchen herbs want six hours of direct sun a day. A south-facing balcony gives them that from spring to autumn. An east-facing one gets the gentler morning light, which suits parsley and mint better than rosemary.

#### Shade

A balcony in shade all day still grows chives and mint. The leaves come in paler and the plants grow slower, but they keep going.

### Part three: watering

Water in the morning, before the sun reaches the pots. A finger pushed into the soil up to the second knuckle tells you more than any schedule does. If it comes out dry, water until it runs from the bottom.

Rosemary forgives a missed day. Basil does not, and it says so by noon.

## Further reading

Any local gardening club will know which herbs survive your winters.
